analysis.one_liner: Bars oil, gas, and mineral leasing in the Arctic Ocean to fight climate change.
analysis.headline: The bill, backed by 8 senators, was sent to the Senate Energy Committee the day it was introduced and never received a hearing, a vote, or any further action before that Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would make it illegal for the Interior Department to sell or renew any lease for oil, gas, or mineral drilling in the Arctic Ocean, including the Beaufort and Chukchi Seas. It declares it national policy to keep those fossil fuels in the ground, citing the finding that most known fossil fuel reserves must stay unburned to avoid the worst effects of climate change. It also protects Arctic waters that support fisheries, migratory birds, and Indigenous subsistence hunting.
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary people benefit through reduced climate risk, since the bill's stated premise is that Arctic oil and gas cannot be developed without busting the global carbon budget. Coastal and Indigenous Arctic communities gain protection for fisheries, migratory birds, and subsistence hunting that a spill or industrial development would threaten. Fishing businesses in the region also gain from keeping fragile ecosystems intact.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Coastal and Indigenous Arctic communities, and the climate

how_it_helps.text: It permanently closes the Beaufort and Chukchi Sea planning areas to oil, gas, and mineral leasing, removing the risk of offshore drilling spills in waters the bill describes as critical to fisheries, migratory birds, Indigenous populations, and subsistence hunters.

It writes into law the policy that Arctic fossil fuels stay in the ground, citing congressional findings that at least 80 percent of known fossil fuel reserves must not be burned to have an 80 percent chance of avoiding the worst climate impacts, and that each decade of delay raises global mitigation costs by roughly 40 percent.

analysis.who_pays: Oil and gas companies lose access to any new or renewed Arctic Ocean leases, and the federal government forgoes the royalty revenue those leases could have produced. Alaska's political leadership, which generally promotes resource development, would lose a development opportunity it has long sought.
analysis.who_pays_short: Oil and gas companies seeking Arctic leases

drawbacks.text: The prohibition would be total and immediate: no exploration, development, or production lease or authorization could be issued or renewed anywhere in the Arctic Ocean, so the nation forgoes any domestic energy production and federal royalty revenue from those waters.

The bill does not address oil and gas development anywhere else, so it reduces fossil fuel supply only at the margin while imposing the entire cost of that reduction on the companies and communities positioned to develop the Arctic specifically.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill trades a modest, well-defined loss — forgone Arctic leases and royalties for one relatively small part of the outer continental shelf — for open-ended climate and ecosystem benefits in one of the most fragile marine environments on Earth. The main honest objection is that a single-ocean ban is a symbolic slice of the climate problem: it stops Arctic drilling without touching fossil fuel production elsewhere. Its design is simple and enforceable, though its climate impact depends entirely on whether other regions and countries fill the gap with cleaner energy rather than different fossil fuels.

outcome.mechanism: It went straight from introduction to the Senate Energy and Natural Resources Committee on July 16, 2015, and sat there without a hearing or vote until that Congress ended.

narrative.text: Senator Jeff Merkley introduced the bill with five original cosponsors — Heinrich, Markey, Whitehouse, Sanders, and Franken — on July 16, 2015.
It was read twice and referred the same day to the Committee on Energy and Natural Resources, whose Republican chair never brought it up.
The action history shows no hearing, no committee vote, no floor action, and no further activity of any kind after the referral, through the end of the 114th Congress in January 2017.
Because the prohibition never became law, the Interior Department retained its existing authority to issue and renew Arctic Ocean drilling leases throughout the period.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Oil and gas companies that wanted access to Arctic Ocean leases are better off, since the statutory ban never took effect and the Interior Department kept its authority to lease those waters. Alaska's pro-development political establishment also avoided a new legal barrier.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Oil and gas companies, and pro-drilling Alaska politicians

for.name: Jeff Merkley
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and recruited six original cosponsors.

for.name: 8 cosponsors (7 of 44 Senate Democrats, 1 of 2 Senate independents)
for.what_they_did: Signed on in support, including Heinrich, Markey, Whitehouse, Sanders, and Franken.

against.name: Senate Energy and Natural Resources Committee
against.role: Committee of referral, chaired by Lisa Murkowski (R-AK)
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled a hearing, markup, or vote on the bill, letting it die at referral.

sides.party_line_note: No vote was ever taken; all recorded support came from Democrats and one independent, while the Republican-controlled committee simply never acted on the bill.

industries.note: The bill would bar the Interior Department from issuing or renewing any lease or authorization for exploration, development, or production in the entire Arctic Ocean, including the Beaufort and Chukchi planning areas. Because the bill died, that access stayed open.

industries.industry: Arctic commercial fishing and subsistence economies
industries.note: The bill's findings describe Arctic ecosystems as critical to fisheries, migratory birds, Indigenous populations, and subsistence hunters; a drilling ban protects the resource base those economies depend on. The bill never advanced, so these protections were never enacted.
